clue.text: Famous Bill, American Democrat leader

parts.note: a bill is a banknote, a note
D is the abbreviation for a Democrat in US politics

explanation.surface: A celebrated Bill, a leading American Democrat, perhaps Clinton.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites thoughts of a famous politician called Bill; instead the bill is a banknote.
explanation.definitionFit: Something noted is well known or celebrated, a straightforward synonym of famous.

clue.text: There are no duds here one has to assume

definitions.text: There are no duds here one has to assume

parts.words: There are no duds here one has to assume
parts.note: duds reads as failures but is slang for clothes, so this is a place where people go without clothing

explanation.walkthrough: Duds seems to mean flops, but it is informal for clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: A naturist resort is a place where people wear no clothes at all, so no duds.

clue.text: Players unable to finish' drink

indicators.note: unable to finish says the word for players loses its last letter

parts.note: a team is a group of players

explanation.surface: A side that cannot complete its match goes for a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea is the everyday hot drink made by infusing leaves.

clue.text: Doctor asked about ultimate in evil enemies he had

indicators.note: about puts the shuffled letters around the single letter
to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are rearranged
ultimate in picks the last letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Doctor Who asked about the evil foes he once fought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' rearranges ASKED to DAEKS, which goes 'about' L, the last letter of 'evil'. 'he' in the definition is the Doctor of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The Daleks are the best-known enemies of the title character of the TV series Doctor Who.

clue.text: I might have found drug in Mexican's modified case

definitions.text: I might have found drug in Mexican's modified case

indicators.note: the drug sits inside the rearranged letters of the possessive word
a case that is modified has its contents rearranged, so the letters are shuffled

parts.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A customs officer recounts finding narcotics hidden in a Mexican traveller's altered suitcase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'modified case' rearranges MEXICANS (the possessive 's counts as a letter here) into EXCISMAN, around which E is placed. The whole clue is the definition: such an officer might find drugs in a case.
explanation.definitionFit: An exciseman was a British customs and excise officer whose job included searching luggage for smuggled contraband such as drugs.

clue.text: Left islet to head east — going north is vital

indicators.note: in a down clue going north means reading upwards, so the run is reversed

parts.note: an ait or eyot is a small river island
a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: Directions for leaving a small island and travelling east, then north.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'going north' means read upwards, so the whole string is written backwards in the grid; 'head' is a headland, not a leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Essential means absolutely necessary, a direct synonym of vital.

clue.text: Something easily done as critic in chat shows

indicators.note: shows means the words reveal the answer within them

explanation.surface: A critic finds appearing on talk shows an easy task.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shows' looks like television chat shows but signals the hidden word.
explanation.definitionFit: A cinch is an informal word for a task that is very easy.

clue.text: Sign in store causes uproar in Glasgow

indicators.note: in places the zodiac word inside the store word

parts.note: a stash is a hidden store
the Ram, Aries, is a sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: A notice in a shop sparks a commotion in a Scottish city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in Glasgow' marks a Scottish word.
explanation.definitionFit: Stramash is a Scots word for an uproar or noisy disturbance.

clue.text: Curse Frenchman's bad English speech

parts.note: mal is French for bad
diction is a manner of speaking

explanation.surface: A Frenchman's poor English accent is a curse.
explanation.definitionFit: A malediction is a spoken curse, the opposite of a benediction.

clue.text: Kiss cheek

definitions.meaning: to kiss and cuddle is to snog or smooch
cheek in the sense of impudence or nerve

explanation.surface: A peck on the cheek.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheek seems to be where the kiss lands, but it means insolence.
explanation.definitionFit: To neck is to kiss amorously, and neck is also brass nerve or effrontery.

clue.text: Anger, say, due to tedious, never-ending function

parts.note: deadly can mean extremely dull, as in a deadly evening

indicators.note: never-ending says the function word loses its final letter

parts.note: sine is a trigonometric function

explanation.surface: Someone fumes that a dull function seemed to go on for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'never-ending' cuts the last letter from SINE to leave SIN. 'say' marks Anger as one example among the seven.
explanation.definitionFit: Anger, or wrath, is one of the seven deadly sins of Christian tradition, so it is an example of the answer.

clue.text: One between about 50 and 100 — an old fogey …

parts.note: re means about or concerning

indicators.note: between says the single numeral goes inside the pair of Roman numerals

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone aged between fifty and a hundred is dismissed as an old fogey.
explanation.walkthrough: The ages in the surface are Roman numerals: I goes between L and C, after RE.
explanation.definitionFit: A relic is, informally, an old person or thing that survives from an earlier age, much like a fogey.

clue.text: … who's recollecting Kentish dictum

definitions.note: the clue continues the previous one, so the person meant is the old fogey of 10 across

indicators.note: recollecting is read as re-collecting, gathering the letters again in a new order

explanation.surface: An old fogey reminisces over a traditional saying from Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this clue to 10 across: its definition is the old fogey there, picked up by 'who's'. 'recollecting' makes the anagram of KENTISH DICTUM.
explanation.definitionFit: A stick-in-the-mud is a person who resists change, which is exactly what an old fogey is.

clue.text: Old truck emerging from motorway junction

definitions.meaning: truck in its old sense meant barter or exchange
a junction where roads meet on different levels with linking slip roads

explanation.surface: An old lorry appears from a slip road.
explanation.walkthrough: Truck is not a lorry but an old word for trade or barter.
explanation.definitionFit: Interchange means mutual exchange, the old sense of truck, and is also a road junction of linked flyovers.

clue.text: Most of the men who fight have more rows

definitions.text: Most of the men who fight
definitions.meaning: soldiers who are not officers, the bulk of a fighting force
additional lines or tiers, taken literally

explanation.surface: Fighting men squabble more often.
explanation.walkthrough: Rows seems to mean quarrels, but it is lines, so more rows is further lines of people.
explanation.definitionFit: Other ranks are all soldiers below officer level, and literally other ranks are further rows.

clue.text: Winning score (by one point)

parts.note: to score a surface is to cut a line in it
E, east, is one point of the compass

explanation.surface: A sports report notes a victory by a single point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winning score' reads as a match result, but Winning is the definition and score is a verb meaning cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A winning smile is an attractive, endearing one, so winning is a synonym of cute.

clue.text: A potential asset with mice around?

definitions.text: A potential asset with mice around?

indicators.note: around signals the letters being moved about into a new order

explanation.surface: A household pondering what would be useful if rodents are about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' is the anagram signal, not a word about mice running loose; the whole clue doubles as the definition, since a cat earns its keep where there are rodents.
explanation.definitionFit: A Siamese is a breed of cat, and any cat is valued for keeping a home clear of rodents.

clue.text: Is Minder broadcast end of seventies or mid-sixties creation?

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered, so the letters are spread into a new order

parts.note: Minder was a British TV comedy-drama of the late seventies and eighties

indicators.note: end of picks the last letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Asking whether the TV series Minder dates from the seventies or the sixties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' suggests television, which suits the Minder surface, but it is the anagram signal; 'end of' takes only the final letter of 'seventies'.
explanation.definitionFit: The minidress was a short dress fashion created in the mid-1960s.

clue.text: Extremely determined to join underworld, like crooks

parts.note: hell is the underworld
bent is slang for dishonest, as crooks are

explanation.surface: Joining criminals in the underworld.
explanation.definitionFit: Hell-bent means recklessly determined to do something, intent at all costs.

clue.text: Wondering if poet has home that's grand

parts.note: Andrew Marvell was a seventeenth-century English poet
in means at home
G is short for grand, a thousand pounds or dollars

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a poet owns a splendid house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grand' looks like an adjective describing the home but gives G, slang for a thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: Marvelling means being filled with wonder, so it is a direct synonym of wondering.

clue.text: Punch given by champ

definitions.meaning: punch in the sense of a sharp, pungent taste or force
to champ is to munch or chew noisily

explanation.surface: A blow struck by a boxing champion.
explanation.walkthrough: Punch and champ look like a boxer and a blow, but they are a taste's sharpness and chewing.
explanation.definitionFit: Bite means pungency or force, like punch, and it also means to chew with the teeth, like champ.

clue.text: Short story writer to have a go at rhyme

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe was famed for his short stories
to try is to have a go

explanation.surface: A short story writer is tempted to try verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' looks like a cut but belongs to the description of the writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyme is used loosely for verse in general, which is poetry.

clue.text: Couple of spots in obscure places

definitions.text: Couple of spots in obscure places

parts.words: Couple of spots in obscure places
parts.note: two kinds of out-of-the-way spot, a cavity and a nook, named together as a phrase describing secretive dealings

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase names two hidden-away spots, a hole and a corner, and as a whole means furtive or clandestine.
explanation.definitionFit: Hole-and-corner describes something done secretly, as if in out-of-sight nooks, so it fits obscure places.

clue.text: Biblical character, not the first to have The Times succeeded in crime

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Biblical character, not the first to have The Times succeeded in crime': AARON less A with S inside gives ARSON, but 'The Times' has no job in that parse and the scan is blank, so the clue as printed is uncertain.
annotationWithheld.clue: Biblical character, not the first to have The Times succeeded in crime

clue.text: Place for dance card in suit

definitions.meaning: a playing card of the suit marked with black trefoils

explanation.surface: A dance-floor venue and a playing card.
explanation.definitionFit: A club is a nightclub venue for dancing, and clubs are one of the four suits of playing cards.

clue.text: One like pike caught in the country way

indicators.note: in places the cricket letter within the road word

parts.note: a lane is a narrow country road
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: An angler lands a pike in a rural road, oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: Pike suggests a fish, but here it is the long spear-like weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: A lance is a long thrusting spear, a weapon of the same kind as a pike.

clue.text: Pet company's service providing food

parts.note: sweet is a term of endearment like pet
RN, the Royal Navy, is one of the armed services

explanation.surface: A pet-care firm advertises a meal service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'service' is a branch of the armed forces, the Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweetcorn is maize grown for eating, a common vegetable and so a food.

clue.text: Very good frame for a door at Oxford

indicators.note: a frame encloses, so the approval word goes around the article

parts.note: OK means all right, very good

explanation.surface: A well-made frame for an Oxford college door.
explanation.walkthrough: At Oxford and Cambridge colleges the outer door of a student's rooms is called the oak; to sport one's oak is to shut it.
explanation.definitionFit: Oak is the university term for the heavy outer door of a set of college rooms.

clue.text: Milk set out for creatures to drink

indicators.note: creatures that drink something take it inside them

parts.note: beings are creatures

indicators.note: out signals that the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Milk is put out for animals to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' is the anagram signal for the three letters, and 'to drink' makes the creatures swallow them, a container.
explanation.definitionFit: Beestings is the first milk a cow gives after calving, also called colostrum.

clue.text: Yelled if kid's ever smacked by heads

definitions.text: Yelled if kid's ever smacked by heads

indicators.note: heads asks for the first letter of each of the preceding words

explanation.surface: A child cries out whenever smacked by grown-ups.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letters of the five words before 'by heads' spell the answer, and the whole clue describes when it might be shouted.
explanation.definitionFit: Yikes is an exclamation of alarm, the kind of thing a smacked child might yell.
